## (1) The Face (le visage) of the Other
The face interrupts our activity and calls us to account; it commands and summons. It signifies, with or without words, *"Do not kill me"* (TI). Levinas describes the face as *"widow, orphan, or stranger"* (Biblical figures encountered concretely) (TI 76–78). The face's expression precipitates transcendence as summons and injunction.

## (2) Ethics as First Philosophy
Levinas argued ethics should be conceived as first philosophy (against metaphysics/ontology), grounded in the face-to-face encounter. Ethics, seeking its existential ground, discovers responsibility in the irreducibility of the face-to-face. (See his 1984 essay *Ethics as First Philosophy*.)

In *Otherwise than Being* (1974), subjectivity's basic layer of sensibility is called *"pre-originary susceptiveness"* (OBBE 122, 136–138).
